meaningMnemonic: This looks like the helicopter radical with something extra under it. It's carrying some kind of cargo. Where's it headed? To Asia . You only know it's going to Asia because the cargo has a big TO ASIA label on it. (Go ahead and imagine it now.) I guess helicopters are the best way to deliver supplies in Asia because there are so many islands and mountains to fly between.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means beforehand . Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: What does your mama tell you to do in the street? Look before you cross! You gotta do it beforehand, or it could be too late.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means business . Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You have spikes growing out of a sheep with fins. Turn this thing into a business! You could totally charge people money to look at it. Sure, you could also donate it to science, but a business-minded person like you knows a business opportunity when you see one. Step right up! Just five dollars for a glance at the rare spiky mer-sheep!

This looks like the shellfish radical, but a little different. It's the mighty crab ! See the eyes and raised pincers at the top, the segmented belly in the middle, and the legs bunched up at the bottom? It takes some imagination, but this spiky shellfish definitely looks like a crab.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means early . Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: When the sun is above the cross, it's time for some people to go church — which is always way too early on a Sunday, am I right? Heck, on Sunday ( 日 ) even 10 a.m. ( 十 )  is too early.

This radical consists of some legs carrying the sun out of prison. Those legs are yours. When the police stop you, though, what's your excuse ? Come up with one and say it out loud, starting with, "My excuse is..."

Do you see the handles on the top and the barb on the bottom? It's a jackhammer . How can you tell? The two diagonal lines on the side show the motion of the jackhammer going up and down really fast, doing what jackhammers do. BBBHHRZHHHHRHHRZHZHHZH JUJUJUJUJU.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means request . Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: Look at the ground! You spilled some water drops, so I request that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?
See the T and F that make up this radical? Those letters stand for tofu , our favorite bean curd blocks.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means together . And see how it kind of looks like two people happily sitting together arm-in-arm? These two clearly enjoy doing stuff together. They're together so much they're practically joined at the hip. Alternatively, think of this as blackjack cards held together by fins. Fish love blackjack because the hands are usually just a few cards, so even fins can hold them together.

This looks like someone sitting with their back straight and a leg stretched out behind them. What kind of pose is this? Probably the kind you do in yoga . Sit on a yoga mat and make your body look like this radical. Nice, you're really doing yoga now.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means younger brother . Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: There is someone wearing horns, holding a bow, and going down a slide held up by a stick. What type of person do you imagine? I'd say someone who's an immature boy. That would be your younger brother.
In Asia they assume everyone's heart is automatically bad and evil . Hints You don't want a bunch of evil in your heart, do you? No, I didn't think so.
readingMnemonic: Luckily, people in Asia know how to get the evil bad ness out of your heart with acu puncture ( あく ). Hints Acupuncture was originally invented in Asia a long, long time ago, to stop the bad chi from going through your heart.

meaningMnemonic: Imagining one’s self without a heart can make it hard to draw breath . Without a heart, you’d have no blood pumping and you would start to die. This would make it increasingly harder to draw breath and get oxygen to stay alive. Hints Imagine trying to live without a heart. You couldn’t. Your blood stops flowing and your body shuts down. You would no longer be able to draw breath.
readingMnemonic: You know how when people are unconscious and their breath slows or comes to a stop, they use smelling salts to revive them? Well a smelly sock ( そく ) can work just as well. Socks get really stinky and their stench is powerful enough to revive someone who isn’t drawing breath. Hints Imagine smelling this smelly sock. Imagine the smelly stench of the dirty sock wafting up into your nostrils and filling your lungs with its odor. Gross.

meaningMnemonic: You stand at a podium early in the morning to practice reading the chapter from your latest book. Hints Picture yourself, standing tall in the light of the early morning. You hold your head up high, open to your bookmark, and read the name of the chapter aloud: "Chapter 42: The Most Important Number."
readingMnemonic: You're practicing this specific chapter because you've been asked to read it for the Shou gun ( しょう ). There will be a bunch of other authors reading chapters of their books to him too, and you want to make a good impression. Hints Picture yourself in a line with other authors, standing in the early morning, waiting to read chapters from your respective books. You really hope the Shougun likes yours. If he does, you'll be famous! If he doesn't, you might be beheaded.

meaningMnemonic: There's a tent of beans . You try to climb it. Hints Imagine this tent of beans. Make it huge, bulging with beans! Now, get climbing. Feel the beans on the other side of the tent's wall.
readingMnemonic: You climb the bean tent, and from this vantage point you can see とう きょう in the distance. Hints It's beautiful! It's breathtaking! All your climbing makes this view of とうきょう even more worthwhile!

meaningMnemonic: The roof , even though it's almost spring , is still covered in ice so it's cold . Inside the house is cold, outside the house is cold. Everything is cold! Hints Picture the entire roof covered in ice. It's supposed to be spring right now, but it's too cold for the ice to melt off your roof.
readingMnemonic: You can't stand the cold anymore, so you hire a samu rai ( さむ ) to come try to hack the ice off of your roof with his sword. You stand outside shivering, and watching as the samurai tries to stab the ice off of your roof. Hints The samurai isn't doing a good job stopping the cold, and soon he and his sword have frozen into your ice roof. So now it's cold and you have a dead samurai stuck to your house. Great.

meaningMnemonic: If a tsunami is higher than your forehead you better move those legs and find a tree to climb, because that thing is deep ! Hints Picture this tsunami rushing past the tree you managed to climb up. It's a deep one, way higher than your forehead, but you're safe here. Legs exhausted, sure, but safe and sound.
readingMnemonic: You wait until the tsunami is only as deep as your shin ( しん ). Then you climb down the tree and wade home in the shin-deep water. Hints Imagine all the debris floating in the shin-deep water now, bumping up against your shins. Probably hurts, considering how sensitive shins are.

meaningMnemonic: A leader who hires his own personal clown will likely double his entertainment. Clowns are funny and make people laugh, so the leader decided to hire one. Since that time, the leader's amount of mirth has doubled. This also means times , which makes sense when you think about the kind of math you'll need to double something. What is A * 2? It's A doubled, first of all, but you're using multiplication. You're "timesing" something. Hints Picture a clown and all the ridiculous funny things they do. Imagine the clown throwing a pie at someone's face and how funny that is. Chuckle to yourself and remember this kanji.
readingMnemonic: When the clown stops being funny, it's time to say bye ( ばい ). At first, the clown double d the leader's entertainment, but now the clown is just annoying. It's time to say bye-bye. Hints This clown has served its purpose. Wave your hand in the air and say bye-bye to this worthless clown.

meaningMnemonic: You'll have to excuse me, having all this power puts a lot of strain and exertion on my body. My power comes from exertion of muscle, so please excuse me if I start to perspire. Hints Imagine yourself under great exertion. You're attempting to use your power to move something and it's really requiring a lot of exertion to move. Picture yourself doing this action and imagine how difficult it is.
readingMnemonic: That thing you're moving that requires such incredible exertion is a ben to ( べん ). It's a massive bento box full of the heaviest foods. Why did you make a bento that requires so much exertion to move? Kinda defeats the purpose of a bento. Hints Imagine a bento box the size of a truck. It's full of heavy foods, like rice and and fried stuff, and cheese… Takes exertion to move this bento, and exertion to digest it.

meaningMnemonic: A long time ago a huge tsunami swept a triceratops up into the moon and extinguish ed its life. Hints I’m sure you’ve heard many theories on how dinosaurs went extinct. Well, this is the real story. Imagine this poor triceratops and all his friends being extinguished by this powerful tsunami, sweeping them up into the moon where there's no air to breathe or leaves to eat.
readingMnemonic: This famous event where almost all life was extinguish ed is reenacted every year for the Shou gun ( しょう ). He's got a bit of an unhealthy obsession with extinguishing life... Hints Watch the Shougun's eyes light up as an actor dressed like a tsunami crashes into an actor dressed as a triceratops and all of the lights on the stage are extinguished. Spooky...

meaningMnemonic: The moon shines down on a stool and a jackhammer which are there for the upcoming festival . Festivals need activities, and at this festival, you can sit on a stool in the moonlight and use a jackhammer to make a lot of noise. Perfect for a festival! Hints Imagine being at a moonlit festival and waiting in line for the stool and jackhammer. You don't want to eat candy apples or ride rides, you want to wait your turn to try out the jackhammer (while comfortably seated on a stool, of course).
readingMnemonic: This festival is for cy borgs ( さい ) only. Picture the cyborg you made getting excited that you're taking it to the festival. That's why all of the activities have to do with heavy machinery. The rides are mostly just cyborgs letting other people ride them, but it's still pretty fun. Hints Imagine your cyborg going to this festival. Everyone here has some type of cyborg enhancement, like robotic arms, legs, or braces. Your cyborg is really excited to be around its people and play with jackhammers.

meaningMnemonic: The village beforehand (what the village was before it was a village) was a field . Hints It makes sense for a big open field to have been what was there before the village was made.
readingMnemonic: On this field , the Ya nkees ( や ) used to play. Hints It was sad that they had to destroy the natural habitat of the Yankees (a field) to put up the village.

meaningMnemonic: Look at a building and compare the white parts. Each of those white parts is a floor . Multi- story buildings have tons of different floors that you can see from the outside. Hints All buildings have white marks that you can compare with the rest to see where the floors are.
readingMnemonic: One floor is just all kay aks ( かい ). You're looking at this building, and every other story is normal, but that one floor is kayak after kayak after kayak. Hints Kayaks working at desks. Kayaks that are desks. Kayaks walking around checking on other kayaks. The kayak floor is quite odd. It's odd there is a floor only about kayaks.

meaningMnemonic: There's a canopy and a man called the Yoga King standing in the middle of your garden . Hints Somehow your little garden is now being used by the Yoga King to teach yoga to a whole group of random people under this canopy... you have no idea how they got back here.
readingMnemonic: Not only is this Yoga King taking over your garden , but he's ordering you to serve food to his class. "You there, peasant, fetch these people your freshest ta ter ( てい ) tots from this puny garden to give them strength." Hints You're not sure what else to do, so you end up serving tater tots in your garden all day to stretchy strangers.

meaningMnemonic: There's a tsunami coming and you want to be together with it by yourself (oneself) so you go to the harbor . Hints Picture the harbor. You're the only one there. The wind is whipping violently and all of the boats docked around you are being bounced around. You can see the tsunami rising out of the ocean and coming for you and the harbor.
readingMnemonic: As you look around at the harbor in your last moments you suddenly see someone in the water. It's こう いち ! He's sitting in an inner tube in the harbor waiting for the tsunami too. Hints Well this sucks. You wanted to enjoy being alone together with the tsunami and the harbor, but now こういち is here ruining your peace. He's floating around in the harbor like everything isn't about to be destroyed, sipping on a fancy drink in his inner tube.

meaningMnemonic: If you loiter around my skin , he will get angry at you. He's my very protective friend, and you don't wanna make him angry! Hints He's already eyeing you down, loitering this close to my skin. Might wanna... back up a little.
readingMnemonic: He may get grumpy if you loiter around my skin, but a well-made curry ( かれ ) always brightens his mood. So give him some curry. Hints Imagine him turning from a frown to a broad smile as he smells the fragrant curry you've brought.

meaningMnemonic: If the sun is on someone , they will get hot . That's just how it is. Someone standing out in the sun for a long time will inevitably get hot. The sun is hot, and it makes you get hot too. Note that this usually refers to hot weather or the heat of an area you're in and doesn't refer to a hot "thing." Hints Imagine you're this someone, standing out in the hot sun. Feel the hot rays beating down on you. You're getting all sweaty and sticky from the heat now, ugh.
readingMnemonic: One sun was hot enough, but then a second one shows up. " Ah, two ( あつ )!" you scream. If you were sweaty and sticky from the heat of just one sun, imagine what this second one is going to do to you. Ah, two hot suns! Hints Feel the hot rays of sunlight beating down on you from two directions. "Ah, two hot suns is more than I can take," you gasp as your body slowly melts into a human puddle of sweat.

meaningMnemonic: If there's a tsunami it's easy to get hot water . Just stick your hand out the window as the tsunami goes by and poof! That water's HOT. Hints Picture the boiling hot tsunami water as it comes for you. Psh, this will be easy.
readingMnemonic: As the hot water comes, you just lift up the bottom of the yu rt ( ゆ ) you live in, and it comes flowing in. All of the cups, pots, and barrels you laid on your floor are now full of hot water. Hints You decided to live in a yurt because of the easy access it provides to hot water. They're so mobile!

meaningMnemonic: A leader of business ? Ha! That's me ! That's I ! Hints This version of I is more boyish. It's a sort of young man/boy way of saying "I," though you'll hear women use it too sometimes (it's a teensy bit tomboyish though).
readingMnemonic: You use the word I a lot. You say it so much, you just start referring to yourself with the french beaucoup ( ぼく ) for a lot. Because you love yourself a lot. Hints I am beaucoup I am. (Is that a pun? Did I do it right?) I dunno. Just say ぼく a lot and try to connect all of your approximate knowledges of languages together. Merci ぼく from ぼく .

meaningMnemonic: A bird sits upon a mountain . If you look at the radicals, the bird is quite large and the mountain quite small. Think of this in the mnemonic as well. The reason the mountain is small is because you can only see the top of it, sticking out of the water. On it is the bird. This small mountain with the bird on it is an island . Hints Imagine the mountain as small as you'd like. Maybe it's only barely sticking out of the sea, and the bird is having trouble standing on it. Whatever you do, make sure you think of it as an island, possibly owned by the bird.
readingMnemonic: But this island doesn't only belong to the bird. In fact, the bird shouldn't be on this island, because it belongs to the She ep Ma ma ( しま ), who is like Mother Nature but for sheep. The all-powerful Sheep Mama comes to kick the bird off the island, because this place is only for sheep! All hail the Sheep Mama. Hints The Sheep Mama is a huge, majestic sheep with magical powers. She kicks the bird off the island with her hooves, and the bird squawks and flies away as fast as it can.

meaningMnemonic: Those who stand on top of a village are juvenile . Imagine a bunch of young people standing on the roofs of buildings in the village. That's a juvenile thing to do. Hints Picture all those juveniles standing on top of buildings in your village, being bored, and doing juvenile things.
readingMnemonic: Mostly, though, the juvenile s are standing on top of village buildings, eating dou ghnuts ( どう ). Hints Imagine looking up to the top of the buildings in your village. Thousands of juveniles, staring down at you and everyone else, eating doughnuts. The crumbs falling down on top of you. But, the doughnuts smell good, at least. Maybe you try to catch some crumbs.

meaningMnemonic: Even a mouth -bearing shellfish is a member of the invertebrate family. Yes, shellfish do have mouths, look it up! Hints Imagine a shellfish opening and closing its mouth, talking to you and telling you what a proud member of its family it is. It's a strange sight, but picture it in your mind anyway.
readingMnemonic: If you were a member of the same shellfish family, you'd be able to go to the special shellfish inn ( いん ). Every species has a members-only inn. Hints Imagine trying to go to the shellfish inn. Imagine all the members-only signs telling you that you can't come in. Womp womp.

meaningMnemonic: A stand ing mustache with legs is able to sell merchandise . Most mustaches can’t stand because they don’t have legs. This mustache, however, does. It also has a keen business sense, which is why it’s selling merchandise. Hints Imagine this mustache entrepreneur, standing at his merchandise stand, selling his wares. He looks quite dignified, legs and all.
readingMnemonic: The mustache is selling his merchandise so well that even the Shou gun ( しょう ) notices. He leans down really close to the standing mustache man's merchandise and stays very still. Then he snaps his fingers and his servants come rushing out to buy it all! Hints Now all of the merchandise belongs to the Shougun. The mustache has nothing left to sell, but at least he's rich!

meaningMnemonic: Someone s and building s, someones and buildings, someones and buildings. So many someones and buildings. With so many someones and buildings, we have ourselves a metropolis . Hints Imagine just a ton of someones and buildings all packed together in a small area. More than a village or town or city. With enough someones and buildings, you end up with a metropolis.
readingMnemonic: In this metropolis everything is a toe ( と ). The someones are toes, walking around. The buildings are toes, too. Hints Imagine this huge metropolis. Now imagine every building just being a toe. Tall skyscraper toes. Smaller house toes. Wide apartment building toes. And then the people walking around. They are toes, too. Toes walking around and going into toe buildings, with toe cars and toe dogs. If you imagine the toe metropolis deeply enough, it should be weird enough to burn into your memory.

meaningMnemonic: When something is heavy , you need a lot of power to move it. It’s not going to move unless you use a lot of power. That thing is heavy and unless you use all the power you got, it’s not moving. Hints Picture a massive 1 ton weight. It’s heavy. You can’t even begin to move it without some sort of powerful machine to help you. Imagine yourself trying to move it with just your bare hands.
readingMnemonic: Remember that 1 ton weight? Well, actually it’s a dou ghnut ( どう ). A huge, massive, 1 ton doughnut. It’s super heavy and hard to move, but it’s delicious. Hints Okay, so you don’t have enough power to move this doughnut as is. In order to move it, you’re going to have to use your superhuman power of eating. Once you eat enough of it, the remainder will be easy to move. Imagine yourself digging into this massive doughnut and taste its fresh baked goodness on your tongue. It’s mighty tasty.

meaningMnemonic: Bamboo 's younger brother is counted with an ordinal number prefix . An ordinal number is one that represents a position or rank in sequential order (like first, second, third, etc.). We use this ordinal number prefix before counting these things in Japanese sometimes. Like with bamboo, going down in order toward the youngest. Hints Imagine a line of bamboo shoots arranged from oldest to youngest. They look like pipe organ pipes, or a xylophone, and now you need to count them.
readingMnemonic: To remember you need to use the ordinal number prefix before you count these bamboo, you dye ( だい ) them. Hints Now they're in descending order already, and you can count them nice and easy thanks to your dye method.

meaningMnemonic: A " crab moon " is a specific period of time . Hints Imagine looking at the moon and seeing a crab on it and thinking: "oh, it's the crab moon time period ."
readingMnemonic: When the crab moon period of time is upon us, we must take a special key ( き ) and lock everything in such a way that crabs cannot get in. Hints Imagine a key with a little crab moon on it, denoting the Crab Moon period of time. Then, go around and lock everything with it and watch thousands of crabs trying to get into everything. Luckily, they can't, because you have a special key that locks things so crabs can't get in. When the Crab Moon time period is over, you can use your key to unlock everything.

meaningMnemonic: If you want a tree to grow straight , you have to plant it properly. Everyone knows that poorly planted trees grow all crooked and twisted. That's just how plants work. If your tree's not straight, start over and plant it again. Hints After four or five attempts, you've finally planted a perfectly straight tree. Pat yourself on the back for a job well done.
readingMnemonic: You plant and re-plant your tree over and over, utterly shock ed ( しょく ) at how hard it is to plant it right. You thought planting trees was easy, so this is a real shock to you. Hints After planting your tree and failing again for the 100th time, you stand there in total shock. How could it be this difficult?

meaningMnemonic: A tree root is still just a root ! Hints Roots are roots, ね .
readingMnemonic: Tree root s are the perfect roosting place for con dors ( こん ). Unfortunately, living on roots is also why they're always endangered. Condors can be killed pretty easily living on the ground on roots like this. Hints Picture a family of condors nestled at the bottom of a tree in its roots. Then a huge machine comes over and mows them all down as it cuts all the trees off their roots. Darn you humans! Do you have to ruin everything?!

meaningMnemonic: If you use an arrow to shoot a stalk of beans , the bean plant will end up short . When the beans are hit with that arrow, it severs the plant in two, and you are left with a stalk of beans that is much shorter than before. Hints Picture yourself shooting this arrow. Imagine yourself nocking the arrow to the bow, and pulling the string back. That bean plant is not short enough, and you're going to do something about it.
readingMnemonic: All this shooting of arrows to make the bean plants short is taking a long time. Since you're out in the sun, you're starting to get a tan ( たん ). After the day is finally over, your tan is really, really dark. Hints Imagine yourself being out in the sun for so long that you get an amazing tan. Your skin feels warm all over from all the sun you were getting throughout the day. Feel the warmth coming off of your tanned skin.

meaningMnemonic: The king request s a sphere ! Hints Imagine the king holding a sphere in his hand, and looking at it. It's a green sphere, and that is because...
readingMnemonic: The sphere is a cu cumber ( きゅう ) sphere. A strange sphere shaped cucumber. Hints Now imagine the king requesting a cucumber sphere, and holding it up to look at it. If you want, have him take a bite out of the sphere, and say "this sphere is a cucumber?" Imagine the taste of it. Imagine the smell, and its bumpy cucumber skin.

meaningMnemonic: White water shoots out from a spring in the ground. Due to the force the water shoots from the spring, the water looks white with all the air bubbles. Hints Imagine these geysers and the white water shooting from the springs under the ground. Now imagine yourself standing over one when the water shoots out. You’d get super wet and probably knocked over due to the force of the spring water. Imagine this happening to yourself.
readingMnemonic: From the spring , a cen taur ( せん ) emerges. Hints Imagine this centaur pushing its way out from the hole in the ground, plugging the water as it squeezes through the hole. Why was there a centaur in the spring? Once it gets out, imagine the centaur standing in front of the spring as it bubbles up and starts shooting water out again. This spring belongs to the centaur.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami lifts all the trash out of the river and it stream s out onto the shores. Hints As the tsunami recedes, watch as all of the trash comes streaming out of the river and crowds the bank.
readingMnemonic: Next to the trash stream you suddenly see Ryu ( りゅう ) from Street Fighter and he looks pissed. He's furious that so many people throw their trash in the river and it causes streams like this. Hints Now Ryu is punching and kicking and tatsumaki senpukyaku-ing all of the trash into burnable and non-burnable piles. But the stream doesn't end. Now he's trying to get his other Street Fighter pals to help him beat it back!

meaningMnemonic: The radical suit and the kanji suit are exactly the same! This kanji can also mean join which makes sense. When something suits you well, like a hat or something, it joins together with you quite well too. Join me, my hat! You suit my head well. It just fit s, you know? Hints Just remember that this "suit" means "to suit you" - not the thing you wear, okay!
readingMnemonic: You need someone who will suit you. Someone who can join you on your life journey. So you call Grandpa ごう いち . Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち . Hints Imagine you two standing next to each other, posing for a photograph. You two suit each other well. Grandpa ごういち with his gray beard, and you with your [well, you have to fill in this part by yourself].

meaningMnemonic: I have sick in my skin . Just look at it, it doesn't look too good. Whenever I have sickness in my skin, I know that I'm probably tired . Hints Imagine yourself being really, really tired. Then look at your skin. It's all blotchy and sickly looking.
readingMnemonic: Why so tired ? Your body is hea ted ( ひ ) up from exercising way too much. You should let that heat cool down so your skin starts looking better. Hints Feel all the heat ( ひ ) emanating from your body. It makes you realize how very, very tired you are.

meaningMnemonic: Stop ! That box of rice is actually full of teeth ! I know it says "rice" on the cover, but I promise you those are all teeth and if you bite into them you'll break a tooth of your own. Hints Stop what you're doing and look into the rice box. Nope, it's definitely full of teeth. There's a grain or two of rice, but it's like 98% teeth.
readingMnemonic: Why do I have a rice box full of teeth ? Hah ( は )! Wouldn't you like to know. Hah! I definitely have an answer that isn't weird or creepy… Hints On second thought, I don't need to explain my box of teeth to you. Hah! Figure it out yourself.

meaningMnemonic: If someone is headed in your direction with a gun , nock an arrow in your bow and gather your tribe behind you because it’s about to get real! This man with a gun is headed your direction and he doesn’t even know what you and your tribe are gonna do to him. If he gets any closer, you’re likely to shoot that arrow right at him. Hints This guy headed your direction with his gun doesn’t look friendly at all. Hear the sound of the bowstring as you nock your arrow and prepare your shot to defend yourself. Then imagine the sound of everyone in your tribe doing the same.
readingMnemonic: When he starts to get closer, you notice that this guy is a boso zoku ( ぞく ) bike gang member. Bosozoku means “running tribe ” and this guy is running right at you. With a gun. So gather your own tribe behind you and prepare to defend yourself against this bosozoku member. Hints You remember what a bosozoku is, right? We wrote about them on Tofugu a while ago. They’re bike gang members and the “zoku” in bosozoku means tribe. Remember that article when you see this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: The direction your gun is facing leads straight to a block of tofu . This might be a sign you need to take a trip . If you're out there pointing guns at tofu, you're probably a little… tired… and in need of a change of scenery. Take a trip! Hints Imagine coming to your senses after shooting up a block of tofu for stress relief or whatever you were doing. Yeah, you gotta get away from tofu for a while… It's definitely time for a relaxing trip.
readingMnemonic: So, where do you go on your trip ? To Rio ( りょ ). You had to go way down south to get as far away as possible from tofu. Ahh, nothing like a nice trip to Rio! Hints Imagine soaking up the sun on the beaches of Rio de Janeiro. Rio has its fair share of guns, but at least there's a lot less tofu around these parts.

meaningMnemonic: People who loiter around the temple are probably just trying to wait . They don't mean to look like they're up to no good, but it's hard to wait without looking suspicious when you're waiting outside a temple. Hints Imagine waiting outside a temple. People are giving you looks. People think you're loitering, not just waiting innocently.
readingMnemonic: As you wait outside the temple, you can't help but adjust your tie ( たい ). When you wait you get nervous, and when you get nervous you fidget. So now you're messing with your tie a whole bunch. Hints Imagine adjusting your tie as you wait. Oh no, now even more people are staring at you. The tie thing is making you look even more suspicious!

meaningMnemonic: There's a tsunami which washes a plate out into the sun . Because it's in the sun, it becomes warm . Hints Right after the tsunami, this plate was wet, but the sun is warming and drying the plate. Imagine looking at the plate and seeing the beads of water evaporate off it as it warms up. Feel the warm steam on your face as this happens.
readingMnemonic: The plate starts to get so warm that you could fry an on ion ( おん ) on it. Who doesn’t love fried onions? That plate sure is warm enough, so start cookin’ ‘em! Hints Imagine yourself frying onions on this plate warmed by the sun. Smell the onion smell as the onion fumes get into your eyes and your sinuses. It makes your eyes water as you are very sensitive to onions.

meaningMnemonic: A horn ed king on a slide catches your eye because you love what he's chosen to wear . sentences.english: I want to be a dentist when I grow up.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

This word can also mean more abstract kinds of movement , like social or political movements that strive for change. It can also be used when describing motion in physics.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Beer after exercising is the best.

meaningMnemonic: For a period of time you have to wait . During this waiting period, you’re building up an expectation or anticipation for something to happen a certain way. readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

meaningMnemonic: The leaf that fall s are fallen leaves .

meaningMnemonic: The essence of your house and garden is your family , household , or home .

meaningMnemonic: Your house tribe is your family . They live in the same house as you and they're part of your "tribe." This is closer than family, though (depending on how you look at family). This is your immediate family because these are the people you live with and give birth to, etc.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: A farming village is a farming village . No fancy, city-slicker mnemonics here. 農村 refers to a rural community where agriculture is the main way of life. Although it doesn't just mean countryside, you'll often see it used in contrast to something else, like 都市と農村 (urban and rural areas).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn 村 's on'yomi with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: Your farming village is so small that it's just you and your son ( そん ). You have a farm on one side of the village, and your son has his own farm on the other side. Together, you and your son form a tight-knit, two-person rural community .

to live in a farming village
to be in a farming village

sentences.english: And people in rural communities are very kind.

meaningMnemonic: Your father parent is your father .

sentences.japanese: うちの家族はみんな父親のことが大好きです。
sentences.english: Everyone in my family loves my dad.

meaningMnemonic: The one floor is the first floor (or floor one ). In Japan, that means the ground floor . Pretty simple.
readingMnemonic: The reading is on'yomi because it's a jukugo kanji. Be careful of the 一 though. It gets shortened and has a little っ in there.

the person on the first floor

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: You know that the kanji refers to a floor (as in the "fifth floor"). This word represents the version that comes after a number, shown with a 〜 . Essentially, this has the same meaning as the kanji you learned, making it nice and easy. Note that floor-counting systems can vary across different countries. In Japan the ground floor is generally called 一階 , with the floors above being 二階 , 三階 , and so on.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Don't type in the 〜 or you'll get it wrong!

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means climb so the verb vocab version would be to climb (or to ascend ), if that's the kind of thing you're into.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. This has the same reading as 上る which you learned all that time ago in Level 1. If you can remember that, you can remember this one!

sentences.english: to ascend in a zig-zag pattern

sentences.japanese: 木の上に登るのは楽しいです。
sentences.english: It's fun to climb on a tree.

sentences.japanese: 山を登るときは、ジーパンをはかないで下さいね。
sentences.english: Do not wear jeans when climbing a mountain.

sentences.japanese: 一生の内、少なくとも一度は富士山に登ることが夢なんです。
sentences.english: A dream of mine is to climb Mt. Fuji at least once in my lifetime.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. This is an intransitive verb. That means it does not take a direct object. Something comes off. Something is removed. No direct object here. That's why this verb means to come off or to be removed .
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 取る .

sentences.english: can get a lot of something, to have a lot of something come off
to be within easy reach, to be easily removable

sentences.japanese: ボタンが取れちゃった。
このシミは取れないかもしれないね。
sentences.english: It might be difficult for this stain to be removed.

sentences.japanese: 丸の内にオフィスを開くとなるとお金はかなりかかりますが、私たちのイメージにとって大切な事ですし、一年ぐらいで元は取れると思います。
sentences.english: Opening an office in Marunouchi would be quite expensive, but it's important for our image, and I think we could recoup the cost in about a year.

meaningMnemonic: I bet you remember 集める means "to collect something." But this time you're not collecting something. Instead, something just… collects. In other words, 集まる means to come together or to gather . Friends come together, or fans gather at a venue — that sort of thing. No direct object needed, since this is intransitive. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある , it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 集める so if you know that word you'll know how to read this word as well.

sentences.japanese: 九州への旅行で全社員が集まる予定です。
sentences.english: The plan is that all employees will come together on a trip to Kyushu.

sentences.japanese: クラウドファンディングで、こんなにたくさんのお金が集まりました。
sentences.english: A lot of money was raised through crowdfunding.

sentences.japanese: 見て！あそこにヤンキーたちがたくさん集まってるよ。
sentences.english: Look! A group of miscreants are gathering over there!

meaningMnemonic: You hopefully remember that 要求 means "demand" . When you make that a verb, it becomes to demand something .
readingMnemonic: The reading is just the vocab word 要求 . It's also the regular on'yomi jukugo reading.

sentences.english: to demand the cancellation of something, to demand the discontinuation of something

sentences.japanese: パスワードを要求する
sentences.english: to request a password, to require a password

sentences.japanese: 社員が休みを要求しています。
顧客は速い対応を要求しています。

meaningMnemonic: You've seen how 落ちる means "to fall down." Now you're doing the action of "falling something down," aka you're dropping it. You can remember this because you kind of toss ( とす ) something and it drops to the ground, making this word mean to drop something .
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 落ちる . So long as you know that word you can apply that reading over here, too.

sentences.english: to drop something into the ocean
to drop something on the ground, to drop something on the stadium field

sentences.japanese: あの、ハンカチ落としましたよ。
そんな信用を落とすようなことは今すぐ止めた方がいいよ。
sentences.english: You should immediately stop doing things that will make people lose faith in you.

sentences.japanese: 今日、『男を落とす方法』っていう本を買ったんだけど、帰り道にどこかで落としちゃったみたいなんだよね。
sentences.english: Today I bought a book called 'How to Make a Man Fall In Love With You,' but I lost it somewhere on the way back home.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means extinguish so the verb vocab version is to extinguish something . You can also use this word to say to erase something , like data, and to turn something off , like the lights or the power. Technically you're extinguishing the data, as well as the lights or power, right?
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to extinguish the fire! The ke ttle ( け ) got too hot, and it caught on fire.

sentences.english: to cross out with a double strikethrough
to disappear, to go into hiding

sentences.japanese: このイラストを消す予定です。
sentences.english: I'm planning to remove this illustration.

sentences.japanese: 間違えてデータを全部消しちゃったんだよ。
sentences.english: I erased all the data by mistake.

sentences.japanese: 教室を出た後は電気を消すのを忘れないで下さい。
sentences.english: After you leave the classroom, please don’t forget to turn off the light.

meaningMnemonic: Do you remember the word 転がる ? This is kind of similar, instead of rolling, this is more for when something falls and hits the ground. It means to fall over or to fall down . Just imagine someone falling off a chair face first into the dirt and making a ぶ sound.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 転がる . Hopefully you know that one well enough to associate it with this one, meaning you can read them both.

sentences.english: to fall down on a mountain trail
to fall down on the sidewalk
to fall down on the street

sentences.japanese: 小さい男の子が転んでしまいました。
雪のせいで道で転んでしまいそうでした。
sentences.english: I almost fell on the street because of the snow.

sentences.japanese: コウイチ、今日は転んでも泣かなかったね。
sentences.english: Koichi didn't cry when he fell today.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means finish , so the verb version is to finish something or to end something . This is a transitive verb, meaning you finish something, like a long day at work! You need to differentiate this from 終わる , which is when something just ends on its own. 終える is about when you make something end. Remember it like this: Canadians always end their sentences with "eh" え , right? Well that's how you know they're ending their sentence. Just listen for the "eh," eh?
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you: You finally finished your school project. "Oh, A!" ( おえ ) you say to yourself, as though you can grade your own project.

sentences.japanese: 五時には仕事を終えて会社を出たい。
sentences.english: I want to finish work and leave the office by five.

sentences.japanese: 王女はケーキを食べ終えるとすぐに、お茶を飲んだ。
sentences.english: As soon as the princess finished the cake, she had some tea.

sentences.japanese: ほとんどの魚は水中で一生を終える。
sentences.english: Most fish spend their entire life in water.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means stream . If you're streaming water, it might be to flush something . Alternatively, to pour something makes a stream of liquid, and to set something afloat is to make something flow in the stream.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What do you do with someone who is a nagger (one who nags)? You have to flush them down the toilet. Imagine someone nagging you to do your chores so you flush them down the toilet, somehow.

sentences.english: to pour water, to flush a toilet
to set floating down a river

sentences.japanese: トイレは使ったら水を流しましょう。
sentences.english: Flush the toilet after using it.

sentences.japanese: そうめんを竹に流して食べるのが「流しそうめん」です。
sentences.english: "Nagashi somen" is where you flow somen noodles through a bamboo tube and eat it.

sentences.japanese: 毎日汗を流して働く労働者たちに感謝の気持ちもないのか？
sentences.english: Are you not even grateful to the workers who sweat and work every day?

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means suffer , and the verb is all about when you make someone else suffer. That's why it's to hurt someone , to torment , or to harass . You need to differentiate this from 苦しむ , which is about when YOU suffer. You can remember that 苦しめる is about making someone else suffer with this mnemonic: Who made you suffer? She ma de ( しめ ) me suffer! She's so mean!
readingMnemonic: By now, you've learned 苦しい and 苦しむ . The kanji in these words all use the same reading! Yay!

sentences.japanese: これ以上、私を苦しめないで！
米不足が全日本の国民を苦しめている。
sentences.english: The rice shortage is tormenting all citizens of Japan.

sentences.japanese: 知らないうちに、毎日一年生を苦しめていた。
sentences.english: Without realizing it, I was harassing the first-graders every day.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 東京 is Tokyo? Add metropolis to it and you get the Tokyo Metropolis . 東京都 is basically one of Japan's prefectures, but they call it a "metropolis" instead. It's the capital and the largest city in all of Japan!
readingMnemonic: The reading is just 東京 and the on'yomi for 都 ( と ), which you learned with the kanji. In other words, on'yomi for all three kanji here.

sentences.english: there are many in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area
to be in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area
to live in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area

sentences.japanese: 東京都は日本の都市です。
sentences.english: Tokyo is a city in Japan.

sentences.japanese: 東京都に住みたがる人は多いですよ。
sentences.english: There are many people who want to live in the Tokyo prefecture.

sentences.japanese: 東京都の３０代会社員、山田さん（仮名）は、インタビューでこう語りました。
sentences.english: Taro Yamada (pseudonym), who is in his 30s and a salaryman in the Tokyo Metropolis, told us this in the interview.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means move so the verb vocab version is to move .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Someone is telling you to move . They are saying " you go ( うご ) over there. Move! Move!" If it helps, have them pronounce "You go" more like "Ugo."

sentences.english: to feel moved, to feel tempted
to move on its own accord

sentences.japanese: あそこで何か動いたよ。
トーフグのサーバーは二十四時間動いているので、いつでもアクセスできますよ。
sentences.english: Tofugu's servers operate twenty-four hours a day, so it can always be accessed.

sentences.japanese: くそ〜。パソコンが動かなくなっちゃったぜ。どうしてこうなったんだろう？！
sentences.english: Shoot! My computer doesn’t work. How did this happen?!

meaningMnemonic: You know that 起きる means "to wake up", but did you learn its secondary meaning, "to occur"? Well, this word means only to occur . Just imagine an incident occurring involving a uranium core ( こる ) to remember that this means to occur . After all, uranium core incidents don't wake up, do they?
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji and the same as 起きる too, meaning you should be able to put together the reading on your own.

sentences.english: to take place throughout the world

sentences.japanese: まさかこんなことが起こるなんて、思ってもみなかったよ。
sentences.english: I never expected something like this would happen.

sentences.japanese: どうしてこんなことが起こったのか、よく考えてみてください。
sentences.english: Please try thinking through why something like this happened.

sentences.japanese: それは数百年に一度起こるか起こらないかの大地震でした。
sentences.english: It was a huge earthquake, the kind that occurs only once every few hundred years.

meaningMnemonic: You should know 開ける by now. This word is similar to that, except it has to do with when things are just open. It's the same thing, though. The meaning is also to open .
readingMnemonic: Do you remember the reading for 開ける , which you learned in level 10? That's right, it's あける ! So if you know the reading of that word (I hope you do!) then you can apply that knowledge here. Just a quick side note — 開く can also be read as ひらく , but we're going to focus on the あく reading here. Since ひらく has slightly different meanings, we won't accept it as a reading for this word, so be sure to enter あく !

sentences.english: a mouth opens (of a person, a bag, etc.), someone speaks

sentences.japanese: このお店は何時に開きますか。
sentences.english: What time does this shop open?

sentences.japanese: 会場はまだ開かないから、とりあえずビールを買いに行こう。
sentences.english: The venue hasn't opened yet, so let's go get a beer for the time being.

sentences.japanese: あの... 社会の窓が開いていますよ。

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

sentences.english: to be able to understand, to be able to stand one's ground

sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんに歯が生えてきました。
タバコのせいで私の父の歯は黄色くなってしまった。
sentences.english: My father's teeth turned yellow due to smoking cigarettes.

sentences.japanese: 電動歯ブラシを買うことを考えているんだが、どれも値段が高いんだよね。
sentences.english: I’m thinking about buying one of those electric toothbrushes, but they’re so expensive.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means plant , so the verb version is to plant something or to grow something .
readingMnemonic: You haven't learned this reading for 植 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You decided to plant an u ni ( う ) tree in your backyard. That's right, you can plant sea urchins and they'll grow like fruit off a really spiky tree. Just picture it. And then you'll get to eat all the uni you want!

sentences.english: to plant something in the mountain
to plant something in the yard

sentences.japanese: ママは庭にリンゴの木を植えました。
sentences.english: Mom planted apple trees in the garden.

sentences.japanese: 町の住人たちは色々な花を植えるのが好きです。
sentences.english: The residents of the town like planting various kinds of flowers.

sentences.japanese: この種をどこに植えるつもりだい。
sentences.english: Where do you plan on planting that seed?

meaningMnemonic: You know that 映る is "to be reflected." Now you're doing the reflecting, which is really projecting (light). That's why this word is to project .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 映る . So long as you know the reading of 映る you should be able to read this one too.

sentences.japanese: プロジェクターで映す

sentences.english: to show a close up view
to bring up on the TV

sentences.japanese: スクリーンにスライドを映してもらえますか？
sentences.english: Could you project the slides onto the screen for me?

sentences.japanese: 他人は自分を映すかがみだと思うんです。
sentences.english: I think others are like mirrors that reflect ourselves.

sentences.japanese: この白いカベをスクリーン代わりにして映画を映すのはどうでしょう。
sentences.english: Why don't we use this white wall as a screen to project the movie?

sentences.japanese: この映画、ここでベーグルをアップ映す意図は何なの？
sentences.english: What's the intention behind showing a close-up of a bagel at this point in this movie?

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. One of the kanji's meanings is sing so the verb vocab version of this is to sing .
readingMnemonic: Awesomely, this uses the same reading as the reading for the vocab words 歌 . Just throw the う onto the end and you have yourself the reading. So, sing your heart out and learn this word easily. "IIIIiiIIIiiiII WILLL ALLllwaYYYs Loovvve YoOooOOooooOOOO ♬!"

sentences.japanese: オリジナルソングを歌う

sentences.english: to sing in a loud voice
to sing at a karaoke club

sentences.japanese: 母は毎日シャワー中に歌う。
sentences.english: My mother sings in the shower every day.

sentences.japanese: 人前で歌うのは好きじゃないんです。
sentences.english: I don't like singing in front of people.

sentences.japanese: 今日は僕が夕食を作るから、君は僕のために歌ってよ。
sentences.english: I'm going to make dinner today, so could you sing for me?

meaningMnemonic: You learned 鳴く means "to chirp" (or some other animal sound). 鳴る is similar, but it's used when something just makes a sound, like a phone ringing, a bell jingling, or thunder rumbling. So 鳴る means to sound or to ring . You know this because 鳴る can also be used for when your stomach rumbles: " rrrr " ( る )!
readingMnemonic: The reading can come from 鳴く . So long as you know the reading for that word you can know the reading for this word as well.

sentences.japanese: チャイムが鳴ったら、教室に入ってください。
sentences.english: When the bell goes off, please enter the classroom.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means suit so the verb version is to suit . This word also means to come together as well. Presumably when something suits something else, it comes together with it flawlessly. That's why this word also has this other meaning (and it will be important for future vocab as well).
readingMnemonic: You want to find a pet to suit your personal style, so you get matched with an a ardvark ( あ ). An aardvark will match the ant mounds you use for chairs and couches, it's the perfect match.

sentences.japanese: 牛肉には赤ワインが合います。
sentences.english: Red wine goes well with beef.

sentences.japanese: この電話番号で合ってますか？
sentences.english: Is this the right phone number?

sentences.japanese: アメリカのインド料理は、アメリカ人の口に合うよう、実際のインドでの調理方法とはかなり違った方法で作られている。
sentences.english: Indian cuisine in America is altered quite a bit from how it’s prepared in India to suit American tastes.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means use so the verb version is to use . If you're talking about money, this can also mean to spend .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You find it quite handy to use two car s ( つか ) in your daily life. The big minivan? You use that for grocery shopping and taking the kids to soccer practice. The little convertible two-seater? You use that one for scoring dates and racing for pink slips. Different cars for different uses, you know? That's why it's best to use two cars.

sentences.english: to attend to, to try to not give others trouble
to use instead of something else

sentences.japanese: 私たちは、毎日電気を使います。
知っている活用形を全て使って文を作って下さい。
sentences.english: Use all of the conjugation forms you know to create a sentence.

sentences.japanese: 今日は青森県のリンゴを使ってパイを作りたいと思います。
sentences.english: Today, I want to make a pie using apples from Aomori Prefecture.

sentences.japanese: このカギを使うとどんなドアも開く。ただし、たまに開けてはいけないものも開く。
sentences.english: If you use this key, any kind of door will open. However, occasionally doors that you shouldn't open will open too.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means wait so the verb version is to wait .
readingMnemonic: You need to wait for your ma ma ( ま ) all the time. You want to go out? You have to wait for mama to drive you. Want to eat dinner? You have to wait for mama to make you food. Hmm. Maybe all this waiting is really a you problem.

sentences.japanese: お母さんが家で私を待っています。
sentences.english: My mother is waiting for me at home.
I'll be waiting at the airport.

sentences.japanese: ちょっと待って！財布を家に忘れたかも。
sentences.english: Wait! I might have forgotten my wallet at home.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means wear so this word means to wear or to put on .
readingMnemonic: What do you want to wear today? How about a dress made entirely of key s ( き )? Feel the metal on your skin and the weight on your shoulders. It's not a comfortable thing to put on. Maybe just stick with wearing a single key around your neck next time.

sentences.japanese: 今日はコートを着た方がいいかも。
sentences.english: Maybe I should wear a coat today.

sentences.japanese: 服を着ないで家を出そうになったことある？
sentences.english: Have you ever almost gone out of the house without getting dressed?

sentences.japanese: 制服を着ると気持ちまで引き締まります。
sentences.english: When I'm in a uniform, I feel refreshed.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 心配 is "a worry." What about the verb version of that? It would be to worry .
readingMnemonic: The reading comes straight from 心配 so try to make sure you know that word so you can read this word! It's also all jukugo on'yomi reading, too, so you should be able to figure it out regardless.

sentences.japanese: 父は兄のことをいつも心配しています。
sentences.english: My father is always worried about his brother.

sentences.japanese: 社長が十一時になっても出社してないので社員たちは心配しています。
sentences.english: The staff are worried as the president has not yet come to work, although it's already past eleven o'clock.

sentences.japanese: 売り上げを心配する時間があるならセールスの電話を一本でも多くしてよ！
sentences.english: If you have time to worry about sales, make more sales calls!

meaningMnemonic: Where the stream is go ing is where everyone's going. That's what tends to be the trend of things. Imagine a trend going on in your society right now. Imagine it going down a stream with everyone following it. This word is also used for less desirable trends, like the prevalence of infectious diseases.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: a trend spreads, a disease outbreak spreads

sentences.japanese: インフルエンザの流行
sentences.english: prevalence of influenza, spread of influenza
a little trend of the moment
signs of a trend, signs of an epidemic

sentences.japanese: ショッピングモールでは流行の服を売っています。
マレットは流行のヘアスタイルの一つです。
sentences.english: A mullet is one of the trendy hairstyles.

sentences.japanese: この冬、お年寄りの間にインフルエンザが流行しているらしい。
sentences.english: Apparently influenza is prevalent among the elderly this year.

meaningMnemonic: When you go on a trip you're taking a trip . This is travel . You should try to do this occasionally! Perhaps a nice 旅行 to Japan?
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to go out on a trip
to set off on a trip

sentences.japanese: いつ日本へ旅行に行くんですか？
sentences.english: When do you go to Japan?

sentences.japanese: 来月、家族旅行で東南アジアに行きます。
sentences.english: Next month, I will go to Southeast Asia on a family trip.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You are going on your trip but you need to bring your little tabby ( たび ) cat with you to keep you company. This cat keeps you calm and lets you leave your house, but the airlines won't let you take it on this trip. What to do?

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of warm ? It's warm .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What do you say when your friend wants to get out of a warm onsen before you? " Ah… Ta-ta ( あたた )!" Yeah, you're not getting out of this warm bath yet — your friend can go on ahead. You just sigh in warm, blissful comfort and wave bye: "Ah… Ta-ta!" People often pronounce this as あったかい , especially in casual, spoken Japanese. The "correct" reading is still あたたかい though, so keep that in mind when you're trying to type the kanji or taking an important test!

meaningMnemonic: Since 話す means "to speak," your way of doing that would be your way of speaking or your speaking style . This includes your tone of voice, speed, and even how you use gestures when talking. It's more about the whole way you communicate, not just the wording or how you phrase things.
readingMnemonic: This word uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned the はな reading with 話す , and the かた reading for 方 is the one you learned with other "how-to" words like 言い方 (how to say) and 読み方 (how to read).

meaningMnemonic: Western-style eat s just means Western-style food . You can call this Western food for short, but in Japan it actually refers to a Japanese genre of food inspired by European dishes. Think omurice (omelette rice) or Napolitan pasta (spaghetti and ketchup). You know, Western- style food.

meaningMnemonic: A leaf of the things you say is like a leaf from a tree of speaking. That leaf is a part of the whole language, it is a single word , though it can add up to be a language or manner of speech .
readingMnemonic: The reading for 言 is one you haven't learned, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Now imagine that there are word s all over your coat ( こと ). It's completely covered in words. Which language are these words in? Why Japanese, of course! Think about which Japanese words you would want written on your coat. Also, note that 葉 gets rendaku'd to ば here!

meaningMnemonic: A writing chapter is just another name for a piece of writing , a.k.a. a composition . Even if it's only a single sentence ! 文章 covers just about every type of writing there is. Although 文章 is pretty versatile, it most often refers to a complete piece of longer writing, like an essay, novel, short story, or poem. But even something super short like a tanka or haiku can be called 文章 , as long as it's a complete work by itself.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
